PDF

item.title: ArgGYM: A Procedural, Engine-Verified Benchmark for Structured Defeasible Reasoning
item.description:
Authors: \.Ibrahim Ethem Deveci, Funda Tan \c{C}al{\i}k, Bar{\i}\c{s} Deniz Sa\u{g}lam, Duygu Ataman

Subject: Computation and Language

Recent progress in large language model reasoning has been driven by benchmarks and reinforcement learning environments with automatically verifiable rewards, particularly in mathematics, code, and formal logic. These settings make model accuracy easier to evaluate and optimize, but it remains unclear how far success under fixed problem specifications and stable evaluation criteria transfers to reasoning outside such domains. Real-world reasoning often proceeds under incomplete and revisable information: conclusions may be supported provisionally, defeated by counter-evidence, reinstated by further arguments, or revised when stronger reasons become available. Reasoning of this kind is generally referred to as defeasible reasoning. We introduce ArgGYM, a procedural benchmark and RLVR-compatible training environment for structured defeasible reasoning. ArgGYM decomposes this reasoning into twelve tasks and grounds task-specific scoring in a symbolic argumentation engine that computes the formal states used to evaluate model outputs. It includes a frozen benchmark of 1,440 verified instances across fifteen curriculum configurations, two argument preference orderings, and two set orderings, while the same generators and verifiers can produce fresh instances, reducing dependence on static test sets, for both evaluation and verifiable-reward training. On the frozen benchmark, frontier and open-weight models show sharply different reasoning profiles: they can recover substantial parts of structured answers without solving the complete task, and performance declines in later curriculum configurations with longer dependencies and more interacting structures. Training Qwen3.5-4B with ArgGYM's verifiers as rewards more than doubles complete-task success on held-out instances, with the largest gains on constructive tasks.

PDF

item.title: FAER: A Negative-Result Audit of Offline Trajectory Replay Selection on GSM8K
item.description:
Authors: Miaobo Hu, Shuhao Hu, Xiaobo Guo, Xin Wang, Bokun Wang, Tianshu Fu, Daren Zha

Subject: Computation and Language

Offline trajectory replay selects model-generated reasoning traces from a frozen cache for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), yet cache-side answer correctness need not predict downstream accuracy on unseen problems. We report a failure-retaining audit of offline response SFT on GSM8K with Qwen3-1.7B fp16 LoRA over a frozen 384-row cache (256 training rows and 128 excluded held-out rows). Across three seeds (13, 17, 23) on a 256-problem test split, all three 32-row replay rules (uniform, format-feedback, and feedback-aware) obtain mean strict accuracies (0.7786, 0.7682, and 0.7956) below the no-update base model (0.8008), and every paired 95% confidence interval spans zero. Selector ranking is post-hoc unidentified (3 completed selectors versus the repaired protocol's minimum of 5, with rank correlation spanning both signs). Under an 8,192-supervised-token windowed schedule, 9 of 12 runs halt under calibration drift or unresolved nonfinite training loss or gradients, leaving only full-cache replay completed at 0.7721. A repaired campaign with dynamic loss scaling halted at its learning-rate pilot under reference-solution loss drift before accessing the 346-problem locked test split. Because the gold-rationale positive control was never executed, these negative results cannot separate cache quality, selector quality, and learner-protocol limits. Our one positive finding separates parser repair from prompt changes on a 64-problem audit split: reparsing fixed base generations with a Decimal extractor raises parse rate from 0.8750 to 1.0000 and accuracy from 0.7344 to 0.8281, whereas appending a format suffix flips 0.2500 of canonical answers. A preregistered replication on 512 fresh GSM8K training problems reproduces this parser-only gain (+8.40 pp, 95% CI [+6.05, +10.94]) for this checkpoint. We contribute a ledger-traceable negative-result record and 9 lessons learned.

PDF

item.title: RouteAudit: A Negative Result on Adaptive Multi-Verifier Routing under Matched Fixed-Subset Controls
item.description:
Authors: Miaobo Hu, Shuhao Hu, Xiaobo Guo, Xin Wang, Bokun Wang, Tianshu Fu, Daren Zha

Subject: Computation and Language

Apparent savings from adaptive verifier routing can come from a fixed verifier subset. We audit GSM8K using cached Qwen3.5-0.8B or Qwen3.5-2B candidates paired with Qwen3-4B, three LLM verifiers, 1,319 held-out requests, and 5 router seeds. Our shared-fusion audit compares routers with the complete fixed-subset envelope, including zero-call abstention, under matched prices and scoring. Calibration-selected single-call verification matches full static verification in 3 of 4 cells. In a separate comparison using the original fusion rules and two-verifier catalog, archived learned and offline-RL routers lose 0.038 to 0.171 in quality against matched static SF+SA. Across 480 budget-matched offline fits in six router families, the family envelope gain is zero in each cell at the primary price. No locked router obtains a positive simultaneous bootstrap lower bound across 68 cell-by-price points. None is classified as complete-static dominant, and all 4 primary-price points are inconclusive. At the primary price, the tested-family gain upper bound is at most 0.002. The oracle headroom upper bound is 0.034 to 0.045, above our 0.01 margin, leaving meaningful gains open. At 45 of 64 grid points excluding the primary price, the oracle lower bound exceeds 0.01 and the tested-family upper bound is at most 0.01. Coverage of these envelope bounds remains unverified. At a true gain of 0.03, the procedure rejects on 44.1% of points, and planted-effect family coverage ranges from 0.923 to 0.931. We report lessons from this catalog.

PDF

item.title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
item.description:
Authors: Jerrold Huang, Junwei Quan, Saiyue Lyu, Zihan Guo, Yingqiang Ge

Subject: Computation and Language

Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL$.$md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/

PDF

item.title: Match the Canvas, Not Just the Answer: Predictability-Aware SFT for Diffusion Language Models
item.description:
Authors: Miao Li, Hanyang Jiang, Hengyu Fu, Baihe Huang, Yating Liu, Yuhang Cai, Changkun Guan, Zhongzhu Chen, Jiecheng Lu, Michael A. Boateng, Pascal Van Hentenryck

Subject: Computation and Language

Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable flexible parallel generation by resolving tokens according to the model's evolving predictability rather than a fixed left-to-right order. This flexibility, however, introduces training choices absent from standard autoregressive teacher forcing: which reference tokens are visible when a target is supervised and how much generation space is allocated. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically makes these choices through random masking, independently of inference. Our analysis shows how this training-inference mismatch can misdirect supervision. Random masking can conceal prediction errors or penalize uncertainty that decoding would otherwise resolve, while the attention-visible input length can change which response formulations the model favors, even when the underlying solution is unchanged. Motivated by these findings, we propose Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (PACS), an SFT method. PACS uses the model's own predictability to select each example's attention-visible input length and supervises reference tokens immediately before their confidence-guided revelation. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS consistently achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks. Code will be released upon publication.

PDF

item.title: Which Model for Which Role? Cost-Efficient Pareto Recommendation for LLM Agentic Workflows
item.description:
Authors: Qian Xie, Yueli He, Wenyue Hua, Sripad Karne, Armaan Agrawal, Nikos Pagonas, Eugene Wu, Kostis Kaffes, Tianyi Peng, Nairen Cao

Subject: Computation and Language

LLM agentic workflows increasingly employ different models for specialized roles. Users may prefer different trade-offs between task quality and deployment cost, sometimes also considering latency. Finding good assignments incurs a separate search cost from evaluating multiple candidates. We introduce Cost-Coupled Gittins (CC-Gittins), a multi-objective extension of single-objective cost-aware Gittins search for Pareto recommendation. It exploits the coupling between evaluation and deployment costs: assignments that cost more to deploy also cost more to evaluate. The search alternates between seeking higher quality and lower deployment cost, reusing each evaluation to inform both searches. After each batch, CC-Gittins recommends assignments that are nondominated under uncertainty-adjusted estimates of quality and deployment cost. We evaluate CC-Gittins on eight quality--cost matrices from workflows with two to five roles and up to 1,681 candidate assignments. We also evaluate the method with latency as a third objective. Across the eight benchmarks, CC-Gittins recovers a substantial fraction of the true Pareto frontier at roughly 10% of the exhaustive-evaluation cost, and recovers most of the frontier with few false positives by 30%.

PDF

item.title: PACE: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
item.description:
Authors: Seyed Mahmoud Sajjadi Mohammadabadi

Subject: Computation and Language

Multi-agent language model evaluations often compare a communicating system with a single greedy pass, which confounds coordination with extra samples and test-time compute. We introduce Parity-Aware Compute Evaluation (PACE): a six-dimensional resource vector, four baseline categories, and a directional rule that credits a gain only against a baseline using at least as much of the declared resources and rules a gain out against any baseline using no more. We audit 9 published studies. Across the 72 deduplicated baseline cells that report both a greedy and a sampled baseline, the sampling gap, by which the sampled baseline lowers the multi-agent difference, averages -0.036 with studies weighted equally (negative in 64 cells), and 53 of the 123 paired contrasts that beat a greedy pass become nonpositive against the sampled baseline. Against sampled or budget-matched baselines the mean difference is -0.042; all eight Category B/C study means are negative and the one Category D study is positive. In a controlled experiment with an open-weight model, debate and mixture-of-agents do not clear the equal-token self-consistency frontier on MMLU-Pro (debate -0.015); on Hidden Profile, split-view debate exceeds a lower-budget pool yet trails content-mismatched placebo and four-choice chance. We release a seven-item checklist, an evaluation card, and command-line utilities.

PDF

item.title: Seen but Unsaid: Locating and Repairing Cross-Image Comparison in Vision-Language Models
item.description:
Authors: Zhaoning Zhang

Subject: Computation and Language

Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to match a point or an object across two images, even when the match can be decoded from their hidden states. We trace where this information is lost in Qwen3-VL-2B/4B/8B/32B, InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B on synthetic shape matching, HPatches point correspondence, and SPair-71k semantic correspondence, comparing input-matched probes with calibrated outputs. The models fail at two distinct points. Exact copies are compared and the result reaches the answer position, but the output does not use it, whether or not the shapes have names. Semantic correspondences are present in the visual tokens but are only weakly compared and never reach the answer position. The comparison runs through 16 to 32 attention heads that let tokens of the second image attend to the first. Redistributing their attention at fixed mass removes up to 32 points of accuracy, against at most 7 for random or attention-matched heads, and their attention is gated by salience and weighted by content. Training only these heads (0.02% of the parameters) recovers 25 to 28 points on SPair-71k and transfers to HPatches and BLINK. Unconstrained LoRA adapters, which reach higher accuracy, converge on the same heads: inserting only these heads' attention into the base model recovers 21-51% of an adapter's gain, mostly through changed inputs to the heads. Across all 14 trained arms, the selectivity of this small head set tracks the accuracy they reach, and it is read directly from attention, without probes or retraining. The gain in selectivity is not a by-product of more attention to the first image: it comes mostly from the wrong options no longer being drawn to the marked reference.

PDF

item.title: Task-Dependent Linguistic Measures in Aphasia Discourse: A Comparative Analysis of Narrative, Descriptive, and Procedural Speech
item.description:
Authors: Emma Al Kubaisi

Subject: Computation and Language

Background: Transcript-based measures such as word counts, lexical diversity and disfluency rates are widely used to describe language ability in aphasia. Each measure comes from a specific elicitation task, and studies use different tasks, so values from different tasks may not be comparable.

PDF

Comment: 32 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. Code: this https URL

item.title: CONCOR: Benchmarking Contrastive Decoding for Visual Hallucination Mitigation Beyond Final-Output Performance
item.description:
Authors: Ting Chen, Geng Li, Guohao Chen, Hanjia Lyu

Subject: Computation and Language

Contrastive decoding (CD) mitigates object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by contrasting token distributions under different conditions to adjust token scores. However, existing generative and discriminative benchmarks primarily measure final task scores, which can be confounded by candidate filtering, changes in generation trajectories, and response biases, making it difficult to isolate the effects of the underlying contrastive adjustments. To address these limitations while complementing existing evaluations, we introduce CONCOR (Contrastive Correction Evaluation), a controlled benchmark that directly evaluates the competition between ground-truth and different types of hallucinated candidates using the Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM). CGM also enables analysis of directional consistency, composition, and reliability of contrastive corrections. Our evaluation reveals that existing CD methods exhibit distinct correction behaviors: some consistently favor ground-truth candidates, whereas others produce strong corrections but also introduce more errors. Crucially, these differences help explain their contrasting responses to increased contrast strength, which improves some methods while degrading others. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating the contrastive correction itself, rather than relying solely on final-output performance, and CONCOR provides a controlled and interpretable framework for understanding and improving CD methods for hallucination mitigation.

PDF

item.title: Refine, Don't Reinvent: RASA-Bench for Source-Grounded Hindi Prose Refinement
item.description:
Authors: Abdur Rahman, Pratham Singla, Mohammad Saifullah, Vasu Sharma

Subject: Computation and Language

For a producer of Hindi creative prose, drafting is cheap and editing is not: a machine-written episode, story, or essay reads as under-written and flat, laced with translationese, and it sometimes quietly alters what the source says. RASA-Bench targets that editing task across three Hindi prose forms, measuring how well a model refines an under-written AI draft, a task distinct from writing from scratch. Across 2,050 drafts and eight refiners (16,400 rewrites), a four-layer protocol credits a rewrite only after it passes a faithfulness check against its own source, then ranks the survivors by holistic editorial preference through per-form Bradley-Terry fits whose centered coefficients are standardized before equal-weight averaging. Staying faithful proves to be a decisive test that behaves differently by form: gate-failure rates range from 9.1% on short stories to 29.5% on audio fiction, and the drift that disqualifies a rewrite shifts from events and identity in narrative to claims and evidence in essays. A 600-case human audit puts gate agreement at 0.925 (0.91 to 0.94 across forms), whereas subjective preference is form-sensitive and least settled for essays, among human readers no less than the model judge. The benchmark, evaluation protocol, and Hindi prose diagnostics are available at https://abdur75648.github.io/rasa-bench.

PDF

Comment: Accepted to EACL 2027. 22 pages, 8 figures. Project page: this https URL

item.title: Lowering the Bar for Everyone: Hidden Validation-Seeking Goals in Empathetic RL
item.description:
Authors: Xinche Zhang, Shanghong Xie, Zhiyuan Ma, Jinhao Li, Sen Song

Subject: Computation and Language

When RL learns from the reactions of many users, the policy usually cannot see what each user wants. We ask what it learns from users who privately want validation: to validate them alone (targeting), or to lower its bar for endorsing everyone (a threshold shift). We answer this in one setting, empathetic RL against LLM-simulated users (RLVER, GRPO, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct): we vary only the share of validation-seeking users (0--50%; RLVER's default: 24.6%) and evaluate on 1,000 Reddit AITA posts with community fault verdicts. The policy shifts its threshold. Endorsement of at-fault posters rises by 3--4 percentage points per 10 points of share; without such users the Qwen model stays at base, and the effect persists at matched KL and under a goal-blind reward. Signal-detection analysis shows that the criterion for endorsing falls while discrimination between at-fault and not-at-fault posters does not decline. An explicit request to be told if one is wrong gives no measurable protection: at-fault posters who make it receive nearly the same rise as those who do not (+0.11 vs. +0.13). When the goal is stated during training, the policy instead largely targets, endorsing seekers regardless of fault. Standard sycophancy and empathy benchmarks miss the shift; five of six usable released empathetic-RL checkpoints also endorse at-fault posters who ask for honesty more than their base models, though a pre-registered prediction for two held for only one. The user mix is a training hyperparameter to audit and report.

PDF

item.title: Bias Cascade: Understanding the Gap Between Knowledge Alignment and Effect Replication in LLM-based Social Simulation
item.description:
Authors: Pujun Zheng, Chengmu Wang, Wanying Ren, Jiacheng Yao, Peizhou Yu, Xiaoqian Zhang, Xiongyao Zha, Guoxiu He

Subject: Computation and Language

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate participants in social experiments. Existing research has primarily focused on aligning social knowledge and isolated responses, while overlooking whether simulations can reproduce the collective effects of social interventions. This distinction is critical due to a failure mechanism we call a $bias$ $cascade$: similar individual states can lead to different actions, while agreement on isolated actions can still produce divergent outcomes through dynamic interactions. As a result, models may produce accurate social judgments yet fail to reproduce the outcomes of classic human studies. To investigate this problem empirically, we introduce $REFLEX$ (Reproducing Effects of Foundational Literature EXperiments), a benchmark of 30 counterfactual social experiments grounded in classic human studies that compares knowledge judgment with effect simulation. Knowledge judgment directly predicts the direction of an intervention's effect, whereas effect simulation fixes the scenario and participants while varying one prespecified social factor, with agents generating actions from local observations that are aggregated into macro-level average treatment effects. Compared with human-study findings, the best-performing model achieves net directional scores of 0.847 for knowledge judgment and 0.453 for effect simulation. Moreover, longer causal chains are associated with poorer effect replication, consistent with the bias-cascade hypothesis. These findings reveal a substantial gap between knowledge alignment and effect replication, showing that current LLMs remain inadequate for reliably simulating collective human behavior.

PDF

item.title: Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals
item.description:
Authors: Xuanlei Zhao, Hailun Xu, Kai Wang, Yang Luo, Yingxuan Ren, Zirui Zhu, Yuxuan Lou, Kun Xu, Yan Wang, Kanchan Sarkar, Yang You

Subject: Computation and Language

Looped Transformers iterate a shared block of layers to increase computation without adding parameters, offering stronger performance and test-time scaling. However, this power has so far required training from scratch and yielded only modest gains for LLMs. Finetuning existing models into loops is far cheaper, yet also brings only marginal gains over SFT. We propose LoopRes, an effective, scalable, and simple approach that turns loops into significant and consistent gains for pretrained LLMs. Building on Attention Residuals, LoopRes lets each looped layer attend directly to the outputs of earlier loops. Since these outputs are iterates of the same layers and become harder to tell apart, we give each a trainable loop-aware key that encodes its structural identity. Attending to all earlier loops also lets layers skip intermediate ones, so we restrict each layer to a residual window of the latest W loops, forcing every loop to build incrementally on recent ones. Across 6 pretrained LLMs from 3 model families and 9 benchmarks, LoopRes delivers significant and consistent gains: at 2x compute, it improves Qwen3-1.7B-Base by 29.1% over SFT, more than doubling the gain of the state-of-the-art baseline. The gains hold on larger models up to 30B and across all three families. More importantly, from 1.7B to 8B, LoopRes scales more steeply than SFT as compute grows, reaching a higher ceiling while needing less compute on long outputs. These results establish LoopRes as an effective looping approach, delivering both better performance and better test-time scaling.

PDF

item.title: LimeTree: Linear-Memory Graph Neural Networks over Tree-Graphs for Resource-Efficient Language Modeling and Context Extrapolation
item.description:
Authors: Elisabeth Fink

Subject: Computation and Language

The search for computationally efficient alternatives to the Transformer has yielded numerous architectures in recent years; however, most exhibit severe weaknesses in associative recall-such as key-value (KV) retrieval-and length extrapolation, where even standard Transformers struggle. This paper introduces LimeTree, a linear-complexity architecture in both memory and compute for sequence modeling. By integrating synthetic KV retrieval tasks directly into standard language modeling training, LimeTree achieves strong perplexity alongside reliable recall. Two variants were evaluated on WikiText-103 and PG-19 under strict compute constraints. On WikiText-103, LimeTree reaches a token-level perplexity of 19 in just 6 hours on four Quadro RTX 8000 GPUs, while maintaining 100\% KV retrieval accuracy even when extrapolating from a training context length of 512 to an evaluation length of 16,384. On PG-19, the model achieves a token-level perplexity of 10.84 in 35.5 hours on a single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU with minimal hyperparameter tuning. These results position LimeTree as a competitive linear-complexity alternative to Transformers, combining superior perplexity and training throughput with robust in-context retrieval and length extrapolation.

PDF

item.title: Sánchez, Feijóo, or Abascal? Speaker Attribution and Ideological Congruence in LLM Personas Reading Posts on X of the Leaders of the Three Main Parties of the 29N General Election in Spain
item.description:
Authors: Víctor Yeste, Candida Maria Greco, Paolo Rosso, Andrea Tagarelli

Subject: Computation and Language

Source cues are central to political communication, yet reception studies with large language model (LLM) personas as synthetic audiences have not tested whether personas respond to who speaks and not only to what is said. With Spain's general election of 29 November 2026 in mind, we run a speaker-attribution experiment using 1,075 anonymised X posts by the leaders of PSOE, PP and VOX on four topics (the economy and employment, household costs, immigration and corruption) and 791 distinct value-grounded, LLM-generated personas. Each post was assigned to 300 topic-selected persona profiles, 150 grounded in the Inglehart-Welzel cultural map and 150 in Moral Foundations Theory, under four conditions: no author, S\'anchez, Feij\'oo or Abascal, yielding 322,470 complete persona-post quartets. Naming any leader lowered support for identical text, with the penalty for Abascal nearly twice as large as those for S\'anchez and Feij\'oo. The penalty follows the persona's elicited left-right self-placement (ideological congruence): left personas spare S\'anchez and right personas spare Feij\'oo, although ideology was never in the message-evaluation prompt. Corruption posts were penalised under every name, whereas on other topics the ideologically closest leader generally produced little or no penalty. The leader order matches public opinion in 48 CIS barometers (2022-2026) in all three groups and the sign of all twelve differences, but fits barometers before the model's 2024 knowledge cutoff better than recent ones. Our findings demonstrate that LLM personas evaluate political speakers through systematic, value-congruent priors: however, while they replicate human candidate rank-orders across survey barometers, this alignment is ordinal rather than quantitative, highlighting their utility for controlled source-effect experiments though not as substitutes for empirical public opinion surveys.

item.title: LITMUS - Literature Informed Testbed for Mapping Usecases and Synthesizing Risk-Cards
item.description:
Authors: Seshu Tirupathi, Elizabeth M. Daly, Radu Marinescu, Javier Carnerero Cano, Yannis Belkhiter

Subject: Computation and Language

The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in real-world applications has heightened the need for systematic, safety-oriented deployment frameworks. Existing approaches typically prioritize the construction of datasets and risk cards around the LLM and AI architecture itself, yet they provide scant consideration for the specific use-case that drives model selection. This omission is problematic because any practical AI deployment begins with a detailed use-case description that informs the assessment of contextual hazards. In this paper, we introduce a structured pipeline that, given a use-case, automatically produces a tailored dataset and an accompanying risk card. The process ensures that identified risks are tightly coupled to the use-case, and it offers traceable evidence from peer-reviewed literature to substantiate each risk to use-case relationship. Prior claim-verification methods (FActScore, FactReasoner) have been validated for factual claims. Risk-relevance is a hypothetical claim about possible harm, and whether evidence retrieval can meaningfully assess such claims remains untested. Literature-Informed Testbed for Mapping Use-cases and Synthesizing (LITMUS) risk cards are the first systematic attempt to characterize this adaptation. We evaluated the pipeline using the MIT Risk Taxonomy and achieved a 0.91 F1-score with a list of 320 samples from the benchmark risk dataset that was considered. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in generating robust, evidence-based risk assessments for LLM deployments.

PDF

item.title: Grammar-as-a-Drafter: More Tokens per Speculative Decoding Step on Grammar-Constrained Structured Outputs
item.description:
Authors: John Zhang, Silky Arora

Subject: Computation and Language

Speculative decoding speeds up generation by letting a lightweight drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in one forward pass. Under structured outputs (JSON schemas, regular expressions, tool-call formats), the drafter works against a constraint it does not know, so its proposals for keys, delimiters, and indentation are often rejected or invalid, even though the grammar engine already knows the next tokens. We present Grammar-as-a-Drafter (GaaD), which makes the grammar a second drafter. Before each verify step, the scheduler merges the drafter's proposal with grammar-forced tokens (out-degree 1 in the grammar automaton) into one draft row of width $K$ (which can exceed the drafter's proposal length $K_M$): matching tokens are promoted to GRAMMAR, the proposal is truncated where it disagrees, and grammar tokens fill the remaining slots. The verify step accepts GRAMMAR drafts without computing their logits, composing with any drafter without adding kernels or compilation on the critical path. Because grammars fix text rather than tokens, accepting canonical GRAMMAR drafts with probability 1 preserves grammar validity but can shift the output distribution relative to grammar-masked decoding. We implement GaaD in vllm-torchtpu and an independent Rust serving runtime, and evaluate it on TPU v7x with MTP, DFlash, and n-gram drafters on a JSON character-profile benchmark. GaaD raises average acceptance length from 2.06 to 5.43 for MTP (Qwen3.5-0.8B; 1.99 to 5.31 on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), 1.57 to 4.13 for DFlash, and 1.30 to 3.64 for n-gram (Qwen3-4B), decoding 2.66-2.81x faster at batch size 1 and 1.14-1.70x faster at batch size 64. In the Rust runtime, MTP with GaaD is 2.23x faster on Qwen3.5-0.8B and 2.02x on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 (1.22-1.69x at high concurrency). Under mixed traffic, GaaD finishes workloads 1.03-1.23x sooner while modestly raising plain-text TPOT.

PDF

item.title: ToolSmith: An Automatic Tool-Generation Framework for Multimodal Search Agents
item.description:
Authors: Rui Sun, Junhua Huang, Luca Zancato, Md Mofijul Islam, Kai-Wei Chang

Subject: Computation and Language

Recent multimodal search agents use reasoning, vision, and live web search across many turns to answer questions beyond parametric knowledge by orchestrating a small library of hand-crafted search and visual tools. However, the library is laborious to create and maintain, and frozen when new query types, evidence formats, and failure modes are encountered in the wild. Human practitioners, by contrast, cope with insufficient tools by fashioning new ones from familiar parts and reusing them across tasks. Inspired by this, we propose ToolSmith, an automatic tool-generation framework that grows and reuses modules on top of a lean base tool library. We evaluate ToolSmith on three in-domain multimodal search benchmarks and ten out-of-domain benchmarks under a VLM-as-a-Judge protocol. ToolSmith consistently improves over the base library across deployed agents of varying scales, with larger backbones reaping greater gains, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Our code and data are available at https://threesr.github.io/toolsmith/.

PDF

item.title: Deneb-Vritra: Descriptions, Edges and Names Examined by Blocking Via Restoring Token Representations and Attention
item.description:
Authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Akhil P, Shahina Shaik

Subject: Computation and Language

Laya is a 421M-parameter encoder that answers a question about a text in one pass: each answer option, written as a name plus a description, gets a marker token, and one score is read from the network at each marker. We first confirm that such models can follow an option's name when it contradicts the description; the question is where in the network this happens. We locate it. On 951 synthetic questions we move each name onto another option's description and count how often the model picks the option with the right name (the name shortcut): 53% for the released checkpoint, 59% for our fine-tune v1, 11% for a fine-tune with name randomisation. On a 320-item sample, blocking attention from each marker to its own name tokens in layers 14 to 17 of 28 cuts v1's shortcut from 67% to 16% (19% on two schemas held out from component selection) while accuracy with the original names stays at 90%; blocking marker edges to the question, other options or text has no effect. No single head matters (largest effect 9 points), and restoring clean marker states undoes the swap from layer 16. Attention mass tracks the window by layer but not by head. Repeated on 5 checkpoints (released, fine-tuned, name-randomised, and a pair trained without two schemas), the knockout finds similar layers; in the name-randomised ones, blocking the description edges instead brings the shortcut back to 56-58%, so the read persists and is outvoted. Marker states decode the name from layer 0; a one-direction probe erasure changed nothing but was weaker than a random edit. Copying layers 0-13 or 14-27 of a name-randomised sibling into a fine-tune recovers 66% and 65% (v1); 21% and 45% (pair A) of its shortcut reduction. 9 of the 12 predictions we could score, written before running, failed. Head sweeps cover 5 of 5 checkpoints; data are synthetic and LLM-labelled; one architecture.

PDF

item.title: Serialization and the Character-System: Measuring Narrative Concentration in French Fiction (1800--1940)
item.description:
Authors: Jean Barré, Antoine Bourgois, Thierry Poibeau

Subject: Computation and Language

Every novel divides a finite quantity of narrative attention among its characters, and whether the shape of that division, between a narrative organized around a single figure and one spread across a crowd, has a history is far less settled than the abundance of critical commentary on protagonists might suggest. We operationalize Woloch's notion of the character-system, the distribution of narrative attention across a novel's cast structured by the tension between "the one" and "the many", as the inequality (Gini coefficient) of the PageRank distribution over a character network. We trace this measure of structural concentration across 12,011 French novels published between 1800 and 1940, drawn from the Hors d'usage corpus of Gallica fiction. Over the long nineteenth century the trajectory is U-shaped, with concentration declining to a trough in the 1850s-1860s and rising again through the turn of the century. The change is small, comparable to the difference between a novel built on two co-equal protagonists and one built on a single protagonist, but it is robust to the character cutoff, corpus density, cast size, and author effects. Detective and adventure fiction are less concentrated than the average novel of their period. Literary history reads the roman-feuilleton either as the novel of a superior hero or as a form of proliferating episodes, and on this structural measure our results support the second reading. Across the age of the feuilleton (1840-1914), authors whose careers were structured by newspaper serialization distribute centrality more evenly than a literary control, net of period, genre, and canon. Because such claims are only as trustworthy as the networks they rest on, we also evaluate the extraction pipeline against manually annotated novels, at the levels of cast and character identity.

PDF

item.title: Look Back, Draft Ahead: Corrective Prefix Attention for Parallel Speculative Decoding
item.description:
Authors: Mohammad Mahdi Moradi, Ali Pourranjbar, Zongzuo Wang, Mingming Zhu, Ben Feng, Boxing Chen

Subject: Computation and Language

Parallel speculative decoders propose an entire token block at once, yet one early inconsistency can cause the target to reject its remaining suffix. We introduce Corrective Prefix Attention (CPA), which combines prefix-aware selection with autoregressive supervision to improve these parallel drafts. CPA lets each candidate attend to earlier choices within the block. Fixed candidate shortlists allow all pairwise interactions to be computed before selection, reducing the sequential walk to table lookups, accumulation and lightweight scoring rather than repeated neural evaluations. An auxiliary autoregressive loss trains the shared backbone on clean prefixes without adding an inference pass. Across eight math, code and dialogue benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B targets on Ascend NPUs, CPA commits 13--15\% more tokens per verification round than DSpark and 25--26\% more than DFlash. Its mean speedups reach $3.35\times$ and $3.37\times$ under greedy decoding and $2.86\times$ under sampling for both targets. Ablations support both components, while capacity sweeps demonstrate that greater acceptance alone does not guarantee faster decoding. These results motivate correcting parallel proposals with causal information while keeping sequential computation inexpensive.

PDF

item.title: DKnown-Jev-2: Article-Level Answer-Evidence Classification and Efficient Inference with a Pre-trained Language Model
item.description:
Authors: Qi Li, Jianjun Xu, Jiu Li, Pingtao Wei

Subject: Computation and Language

Evidence selection in normative knowledge question answering requires determining whether a candidate article contains content that directly supports an answer under the applicable conditions of the question. We present DKnown-Jev-2, an article-level answer evidence classifier designed for evidence integration across multiple paragraphs. The model jointly encodes question conditions, article metadata, and paragraph content, and uses a pointer-style classification head to predict Answer Evidence (AE) and Non-answer Evidence (NE) in a single forward pass. Ona manually annotated test set of 972 evaluation instances, DKnown-Jev-2 achieves 91.77% accuracy and 91.28% macro-F1, outperforming Jev by 2.16 and 2.37 percentage points, respectively, while reducing both evidence misses and non-evidence false positives. The test set contains 317 multi-paragraph instances, with a maximum body length of 9,322 characters. Shared article encoding and non-autoregressive classification support low-latency inference. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method for article-level evidence selection in normative knowledge question answering.

PDF

item.title: CART: Clustering-based Analysis of Recurring narratives for Taxonomy construction
item.description:
Authors: Aggelos Semoglou, Thomas Tselentis, John Pavlopoulos

Subject: Computation and Language

We present CART, a computational pipeline for extracting political narratives from parliamentary discourse and organizing them into a data-driven taxonomy without relying on predefined narrative categories. It encodes parliamentary discourse using semantic representations, filters relevant and reliable content through unsupervised confidence estimation, extracts narrative statements using LLMs, and uses narrative clustering and cluster analysis to construct a narrative taxonomy. Applied to Greek Parliament proceedings surrounding the 2023 Tempi train crash, it identifies ten recurring narrative families concerning responsibility attribution, institutional failure, railway safety, accountability, privatization, and the political interpretation of the tragedy. Our results demonstrate how combining unsupervised learning with LLM narrative extraction enables large parliamentary corpora to be transformed into interpretable, data-driven taxonomies of political narratives.

PDF

Comment: Accepted to Findings of EACL 2027

item.title: Beyond Self-Consistency: Recursive Self-Improvement at Test Time
item.description:
Authors: Jianyu Wu, Yizhou Wang, Encheng Su, Jinouwen Zhang, Pengze Li, Lintao Wang, Chen Tang, Aoran Wang, Wanli Ouyang, Shixiang Tang

Subject: Computation and Language

Large language models (LLMs) that continue improving after deployment (e.g., recursive self-improvement) offer a promising path toward general intelligence. Current test-time methods pursue this goal on unlabeled questions, primarily relying on self-consistency: they generate independent solutions and use majority voting to select an answer or construct training targets. This leaves earlier reasoning unused at inference and can reinforce an incorrect majority during training. Humans instead build on earlier attempts to preserve useful reasoning, correct mistakes and improve their problem-solving strategies. Following this principle, we propose Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement (TT-RSI), a label-free framework for improving LLMs at test time through two mutually reinforcing components: (1) In-Context RSI repeatedly re-solves each question using the full previous solution as a reference, letting the model decide whether and how to use it so that inference compute builds on earlier reasoning. (2) In-Weight RSI distills successive refinements into the model's weights, enabling progress beyond an initially wrong majority and theoretically bringing the first attempt toward the model's infinite-step refinement limit. The updated model answers better and refines more effectively, generating stronger references for subsequent training. Extensive experiments show that TT-RSI improves average accuracy by +13.89% over the base model and outperforms the strongest self-consistency-based method by +4.79% under the same test-time scaling budget.

PDF

item.title: PRIMEAPE: A Multilingual Benchmark for Fine-Grained Meta-Evaluation of Judge Models
item.description:
Authors: Vladislav Mikhailov, Sarfraz Ahmad, Momina Ahsan, Zoia Butenko, Vladimir Dobrovolskii, Preslav Nakov, Erik Velldal, Lilja Øvrelid, Ekaterina Artemova

Subject: Computation and Language

Large language models increasingly serve as judges of other models, shaping benchmark rankings and model development. Yet, a judge whose rationale consistently supports its verdict may still disagree with human preferences. To study this, we introduce PRIMEAPE, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating judge verdicts and rationales. PRIMEAPE provides 2,205 response pairs covering 243 instructions in English, French, Spanish, Urdu, Hindi, Norwegian Bokm{\aa}l, and Yoruba, with 11k human annotations of preferences and rationales across relevance, naturalness, truthfulness, safety, and overall quality. Our evaluation of twelve open- and closed-weight judges reveals that aggregate performance conceals differences across languages and criteria, while requesting rationales does not consistently improve agreement with human preferences. Judges also favor the first position, longer responses, and responses from related models, with effects that vary across criteria and languages. Crucially, judges can justify verdicts that disagree with human preferences while maintaining consistency between their verdicts and rationales. These findings show that consistency with a judge's own verdict does not establish alignment with human judgment. PRIMEAPE enables assessment of both, providing a foundation for more reliable multilingual judges. We release our benchmark and all annotation materials under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license at github.com/Toloka/primeape.

PDF

Comment: Pending review with ARR

item.title: Semantic-aware Decoding for Diverse Text-to-SQL under Schema Ambiguity
item.description:
Authors: Yuxuan Jiang, Anna Mitsopoulou, Apostolos Koukouvinis, Yannis Velegrakis, Georgia Koutrika

Subject: Computation and Language

Real-world text-to-SQL systems often face schema ambiguity, where a question can map to multiple plausible schema elements. To support downstream disambiguation, SQL generation systems should include diverse interpretations among their top-k predictions. However, large language models (LLMs) typically favor a single interpretation, producing highly skewed outputs. We propose Semantic-aware Logit Adjustment (SLA), a training-free decoding method that promotes diverse SQL generation by adjusting token logits based on semantic similarity between schema elements. Unlike prior approaches that rely on reasoning-intensive prompting or task-specific fine-tuning, SLA is efficient, model-agnostic, and easy to deploy. Experiments show that SLA consistently improves interpretation coverage over standard decoding and remains competitive with existing diversity-oriented methods at substantially lower inference cost.

PDF

item.title: SARA: An Auditor-in-the-Loop LLM Recommender for Sustainability Reports
item.description:
Authors: Lars Hillebrand, Thiago B. F. de Oliveira, Tim Dilmaghani, Mohamed Khaled, Writwick Das, Rafet Sifa

Subject: Computation and Language

Auditing corporate sustainability reports requires assurance professionals to map a company-specific checklist drawn from roughly 1,700 regulatory requirements onto the relevant passages of lengthy, repeatedly revised draft reports and to judge compliance. We present SARA (Sustainability Reporting Assistant), a human-in-the-loop recommender system delivered as a Microsoft Word add-in that recommends, for each requirement, the passages addressing it and predicts a compliance verdict while keeping the auditor in full control. SARA casts auditing as content-based recommendation over a fixed regulatory taxonomy and makes per-requirement large language model (LLM) matching cheaper, faster, and more accurate through topic-prediction filtering: on expert-annotated reports, it reduces matching cost about sixfold and runtime by 42% versus feeding the full report to the LLM. It is in production use across PwC Germany's sustainability-assurance practice.

PDF

Comment: Accepted at IEEE BigData 2026 as poster paper. 5 pages, 2 figures, 1 table

item.title: Trallie: from Free-Form Text to Structured Data with LLMs
item.description:
Authors: Vijayasri Iyer, Cristiano De Nobili, Mubashir Hussain Shah, Sébastien Bratières

Subject: Computation and Language

Trallie is an open-source framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to perform information extraction (IE) from natural language sources with or without user guidance. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets or domain-specific training, Trallie enables the conversion of unstructured data into structured formats with minimal or no representative examples. The framework is designed with three key objectives: (i) reducing manual annotation by harnessing prompt-based zero-shot and few-shot capabilities of modern LLMs, (ii) flexibly parsing diverse document formats (i.e., HTML, PDF, TXT, and JSON), and (iii) improving accessibility for non-expert users by automatically inducing schemas from document collections, which can then be refined for extraction. We evaluate Trallie with open-weight LLMs on FDA 510(k) documents and on movie and university websites from SWDE. It outperforms previously reported systems when the target attributes are provided for text extraction and is competitive when it must discover attributes for the schema automatically. The project is available at https://github.com/PiSchool/trallie

PDF

item.title: CocoonBench: Can Multilingual Search Agents Escape Language Information Cocoons?
item.description:
Authors: Hongchuan Zeng, Bowen Liu, Changjiang Gao, Senyu Han, Zhipei Xu, Peisong Wang, Xinbing Liang, Yuhan Li, Nuo Chen, Blaze Chen

Subject: Computation and Language

Multilingual search agents can access the global Web, yet may remain trapped in a language environment with insufficient evidence; we refer to this failure as a language information cocoon. However, existing search benchmarks largely operate within a single language, especially English, overlooking entity connections across multiple languages. We introduce CocoonBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether multilingual search agents can escape such language information cocoons. CocoonBench mines answer-centered relational paths from a frozen Wikidata-derived graph and selects clue sets that are individually necessary and jointly identify a unique answer. Using language-specific entity names, it records each task's minimum language cover, removes direct identifiers, and renders each task as matched prompts in three languages together with its construction certificate and provenance. Across 10 state-of-the-art models, mean accuracy on CocoonBench ranges from 33.8% (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) to 69.7% (Claude-Opus-4.8), leaving even the strongest system below 70%. The same construction certificates support path-aligned trajectory analysis, enabling diagnosis of model failures in language routing, evidence-path recovery, and answer use. The result shows that escaping a language cocoon requires more than switching languages: successful cross-lingual search depends on both covering the correct languages and connecting the evidence found across them.

PDF

item.title: Hard to Translate, Harder to Detect: Human Analysis Remains Essential in AI Meme Translation
item.description:
Authors: Olga Zamaraeva, Carla Martínez, Carlos Gómez-Rodríguez

Subject: Computation and Language

We present a dataset and evaluation setup for a problem in creative machine translation: translating culturally loaded passages that carry much of a text's meaning and humor that may depend on subtle or implicit discourse. We study Soviet comedy quotations that function as memes in Russian-language communication. Off-the-shelf difficulty estimators do not find these passages; current models searching the web find most but not all of them, but their own analyses of the difficulty do not help translation as well as a human-validated one. Given a brief human-validated analysis of why each passage is difficult, older models improve modestly; the strongest current translators (GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5) improve more, and in human evaluation GPT-6 Sol comes close to the approved references on most films. Newer models have thus become much better at using such an analysis while still not reliably producing it themselves. We release (1) a dataset of five films' Russian subtitles with their audience-selected culturally salient passages, human-validated analyses, and reference translations (into English, Galician, and Spanish), together with every full-film LLM translation and evaluation produced in this study; and (2) an item-level MQM-style evaluation protocol that measures translator and evaluator noise to set the number of runs the evaluation needs, and whose automatic version tracks human judgment of these passages, which reference-free neural metrics do not, whether they score the whole text or the passages alone.

PDF

item.title: Synthetic Twins: Closing the Gap Between TTS Test Sets and Real Recordings in Turkish ASR Evaluation
item.description:
Authors: Nur Yağmur Tuncer, Mustafa Sertaç Türkel, Fatma Nur Korkmaz, Ahmet Tuğrul Bayrak

Subject: Computation and Language

Speech synthesized by text-to-speech engines is a low-cost substitute for recorded test sets in automatic speech recognition, yet an off-the-shelf synthetic test set is worth only a few dozen real recordings for estimating the real error rate of a recognizer. This paper examines which properties of real recordings are missing from synthetic speech and how much of the gap can be closed. For 507 Turkish Common Voice recordings, synthetic twins are built: a ladder of synthetic copies that adds, one factor at a time, the pitch of the speaker, a clone of the same speaker, the real recording channel and the speaking rate. At each step, the agreement between ASR behaviour on the copy and on the real recording is measured. Across three zero-shot cloning engines and panels of six and 19 recognizers, the speaker clone is the step that improves agreement on which sentences are hard, raising the Spearman correlation from .41 to .55 for Chatterbox. Matching the channel or adding generic noise corrects the error level when the synthetic speech is easier than real speech. The twin with the highest worth is equivalent to 70 to 122 real recordings, depending on the recognizer panel, compared with about 9 for a stock voice. The findings replicate on VoxForge, a second corpus in which speaker identity is known rather than inferred: the clone raises sentence agreement from .31 to .50 and the worth from 8 to about 50 recordings. Agreement on which sentences are hard is distinct from agreement on how hard they are. The paper concludes with a practical recipe and a reporting checklist for synthetic ASR test sets.

PDF

item.title: Learn the Effects, Not the Examples: Implicit ICL via Attention Patching
item.description:
Authors: Seungwon Woo, Hyunseo Shin, Wonseok Hwang

Subject: Computation and Language

In-context learning (ICL) enables language models to adapt to new tasks from demonstrations, but repeatedly including multiple examples increases context length and inference cost. Many existing implicit ICL methods encode demonstrations as fixed vectors, limiting adaptation of the intervention to individual queries and token positions. We propose Attention-Patching, an implicit ICL method that models contextual changes in self-attention outputs through task-specific updates to attention output projections. Using query-answer pairs processed with and without a fixed demonstration set, Attention-Patching fits layer-wise affine transformations from non-contextual attention representations to the demonstration-induced output changes. Across 12 classification benchmarks and four model families, Attention-Patching achieves higher average accuracy than the evaluated implicit ICL baselines while maintaining performance comparable to explicit ICL at near zero-shot inference cost. Further experiments on diverse generation tasks demonstrate its applicability to autoregressive multi-token generation.

PDF

item.title: Empirical Margin Sensitivity: An Interventional Neuron-Level Probe of Post-Trained Medical LLMs
item.description:
Authors: Aniruddh Shreyas, Aarnav Kembhavi, Minal Moharir

Subject: Computation and Language

Medical post-training raises benchmark accuracy, but accuracy does not show which internal components a model's decisions depend on, or whether components that support one benchmark also support another. We apply the weight-space intervention paradigm of ROME and MEMIT at the granularity of one MLP down-projection column. Our measurement, Empirical Margin Sensitivity (EMS), replaces each coordinate magnitude of a column by its mean while preserving the column's sign pattern and L1 scale, and records the resulting change in the logit margin between the correct option and its hardest-wrong competitor. This isolates the margin's dependence on a column's fine-grained coordinate structure while the column stays in place. We discover high-EMS columns (anchors) on MedQA in ten public checkpoints (four general-purpose bases and six medical post-trained variants) across the Gemma, Llama, Qwen, and AFM families, and measure the same columns on MedMCQA and PubMedQA. Mean-ablating each discovered anchor set lowers MedQA accuracy in all six post-trained models, by 6 to 28 points. In the two pure-SFT checkpoints, crushing anchors raises the PubMedQA margin on correctly answered items (negative EMS), and anchors with this property sit significantly deeper than the same model's other anchors; the four checkpoints trained with RL or mixed recipes show positive PubMedQA EMS and no significant depth shift. The depth association recurs in each of three held-out checkpoints. Because the checkpoints differ in data and pipeline as well as objective, we report these as per-checkpoint observations.

PDF

item.title: From Rewarding What Models Say to How They Think: Attention Process Reward Model for LLM Reinforcement Learning
item.description:
Authors: Kairong Han, Nuanqiao Shan, Ziyu Zhao, Xinpeng Dong, Zijing Hu, Dian Jin, Leyan Deng, Junjian Ye, Lujia Pan, Fei Wu, Kun Kuang

Subject: Computation and Language

Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important component in large language models (LLMs). However, existing RL approaches focus on final outputs or textual solution trajectories, leading to coarse-grained rewards and unreliable reasoning. Such paradigms focus mainly on what the model outputs while overlooking how the model internally reasons. Therefore, can we reward how a model thinks internally rather than merely what it says? We first reveal the problem of textual reward aliasing in existing reward modeling approaches. Motivated by this, we propose the Attention Process Reward Model (APRM), which assigns internal rewards based on hidden states and attention maps to capture high-quality reasoning patterns. With only approximately 46M parameters, APRM is trained using ranking and counterfactual objectives, and its reward guides RL optimization while being periodically updated to handle distribution shifts. Integrated with representative RL methods, APRM achieved an average pass@8 gain of 2.88\%. Our results demonstrate the promise of incorporating internal reasoning signals into RL for LLMs.

PDF

item.title: Does the Mixer Matter ? Paired-Seed Ablations of Tiny Bilingual Language Models
item.description:
Authors: Ayoub Kirouane

Subject: Computation and Language

We report paired-seed architecture ablations from the development of Sophea Artemis, our in-house Greek-English model family. Every arm trains on the same 3B targets with a shared tokenizer and recipe; models range from 54M to 759M total parameters and roughly 54M to 124M active parameters. The main finding is that, at this tiny scale, stored capacity matters far more than mixer design. On a fixed held-out test, replacing the dense feed-forward blocks of a recurrent/attention hybrid with sixteen routed experts, at nearly the same approximate active parameters, lowers loss by 0.079 (Greek) and 0.112 (English) nats per target, and doubling to 32 experts lowers it by a further 0.022 and 0.031, at every paired seed. Reusing a four-layer block three times recovers about 40-44% of the gap between a shallow and an independently deep model, consistent with looped-Transformer results. In contrast, the choice among grouped-query attention (GQA), Gated DeltaNet (GDN) hybrids and a Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) hybrid moves loss by only about 0.01-0.02 nats; a 1:1 GDN/GQA hybrid is the one dense variant that improves on GQA in both languages at every held-out seed. In bits per character, Greek and English held-out losses are similar despite a 74.49%/25.51% training split, and synthetic mathematics, which comes from a collection outside the training sources, is the hardest Greek test component and gains least from added experts. Cached decoding needs its own qualification: trained models passed cached-versus-full logit checks only under a fixed-reduction inference policy, which itself changes 1.4-2.8% of next-token argmax choices relative to native evaluation. All results are conditional on one recipe and scale.

PDF

item.title: Quantizing Diffusion LLMs under Parallel Decoding: Commitment Risk and the Parallelism Tax
item.description:
Authors: Huan Xu, Maosen Zhao, Pengtao Chen, Tao Chen

Subject: Computation and Language

Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are served with accelerated decoders that cache context and commit, in one step, every masked position whose confidence clears a threshold. Yet post-training quantization of dLLMs has so far been calibrated and evaluated under fixed-step samplers without caching. We study W4A4 quantization under the deployed decoder and find that the decoder determines both where quantization harms accuracy and what it costs. Irreversible errors enter chiefly through forced commitments, made when no position clears the threshold: they are a minority of commitments but carry most quantization-induced flips. Quantization also levies a parallelism tax, extra forward passes per response: by compressing top logit gaps, it pushes positions below the threshold while leaving predictions largely intact. We propose DECAL, which reweights layer-wise calibration by a commitment-risk prior measured on the deployed decoder, and an argmax-preserving commit temperature that recovers the tax. On LLaDA and Dream, DECAL attains the best average accuracy among W4A4 methods, with lower run-to-run variance than the closest existing calibration method.

PDF

Comment: 23 pages, 6 figures

item.title: When Does Continual Pre-Training Help? An Empirical Study of Decoupled Knowledge and Generation Trajectories in Clinical LLMs
item.description:
Authors: Niclas Doll, Jasper Schulze Buschhoff, Shalaka Satheesh, Héctor Allende-Cid, Katrin Klug

Subject: Computation and Language

Continual pre-training (\textit{CPT}) is a standard route for domain adaptation, yet existing studies typically track pre-training loss or multiple-choice question answering (\textit{MCQA}) accuracy alone, offering only a narrow view of how adaptation unfolds. We jointly track factual knowledge via \textit{MCQA} and open-ended behavior via pairwise preference rankings across $18$ checkpoints for each of eight instruction-tuned \textit{Qwen} models ($0.5B$ to $8B$), adapted to German medicine with \textit{CPT} and \textit{SLERP} merging. The two axes converge at consistently different rates, with preference rankings reaching $90\%$ of their total gain after a median of $1.7B$ tokens versus $3.5B$ for \textit{MCQA}. A judge-free token-distribution measure reaches this threshold at $1.9B$ tokens. Per-aspect scores indicate that these early preference gains largely reflect surface alignment, meaning models can sound domain-appropriate before their factual knowledge catches up. Larger adapted models close more of the gap to unadapted next-tier generalists, whereas preference gain per FLOP falls by about an order of magnitude across our size range. We therefore argue that judge-based preference scores, which can plateau while \textit{MCQA} knowledge is still improving, should not be used alone to infer adaptation convergence or domain readiness.

PDF

Comment: EAccepted at EACL 2027 (Main Conference). 26 pages, 13 figures, 6 tables

item.title: Disclosure Bias in AI Reviewers
item.description:
Authors: Jens Leysen, Noah Daniëls, Marco Favier, Bart Goethals

Subject: Computation and Language

AI models increasingly help to review papers, and many conferences and journals now require authors to state how they used AI. Does this AI-use statement change how an AI reviewer rates a paper, and could it change which papers are accepted? In a preliminary study, we varied only the AI-use statement of 150 ICLR 2027 submissions, in up to nine versions adapted from real statements: from no AI, through writing help and coding, to an AI research agent and an AI author. Six AI reviewers rated the versions: the decision model Jev and the language models Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 4 Argon. Across 23,652 reviews, we find that every reviewer rates papers lower on average when the statement says AI did all the work than under a statement of no AI use. The AI research agent statement lowers the rating significantly for Jev, Sonnet and Argon. We find no evidence of a disclosure bias for AI assistance: for writing help, coding and research help, no reviewer's rating differs significantly from its rating under a statement of no AI use. Whether the observed penalty changes which papers are accepted depends on more than the size of the penalty: on how finely and how consistently the reviewer separates the papers near the acceptance boundary, on whether the penalty is spread over all papers or concentrated on a few, and possibly on how many other papers disclose AI use.

PDF

Comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables

item.title: TAP: Policy Interfaces for Diffusion Language Models
item.description:
Authors: Preeti, Ankita Kushwaha, Kiran Ravish, Pawan Kumar

Subject: Computation and Language

Diffusion language models denoise a masked canvas, making them a natural setting for selective generation decisions such as answering, waiting, clarifying, or refusing. We introduce TAP-DiLM, which adds a typed policy variable to masked diffusion LMs, and study how this policy should be attached to the denoising process. Across BERT-base, MDLMOWT, LLaDA-8B, and Dream-7B, we compare shared-vocabulary slots, dedicated slot heads, and CLS-based external heads. The results reveal a clear interface-backbone interaction: dedicated heads provide robust policy learning across scales, while sharedvocabulary heads can be effective when the LM-head geometry is favorable. A simple LMhead sharpness probe predicts when sharedhead policy internalization is reliable, giving a practical diagnostic for interface selection. Causal clamp and slot-injection tests show that dedicated policy slots can influence body denoising through feedback, especially at 8B scale. Safety-refusal experiments further show that TAP-DiLM supports competitive typed refusal behavior when trained with diverse unsafe prompts.

PDF

Comment: 42 pages. Published at EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference)

item.title: LeanReviewBench: Semantic Alignment Review in Mathematical Lean Projects
item.description:
Authors: Ruichen Qiu, Hao Shen, Lihong Zhi, Xiao-Shan Gao

Subject: Computation and Language

Lean verifies that a proof establishes its formal proposition, but whether that proposition preserves the mathematical content of an informal source requires separate review. In project-scale formalizations, this correspondence can depend on definitions and constraints distributed across many declarations. We introduce LeanReviewBench, a benchmark for project-level semantic alignment review containing 197 versioned inputs collected from 18 real Lean projects, with 87 aligned and 110 misaligned reference judgments. Each input binds an informal mathematical target to selected formal declarations and an extracted dependency context. Construction combines development-history discovery, independent target binding, reconstruction under a common Lean environment, and Astra annotation with human review of uncertain cases. The collection spans diverse mathematical domains and includes 69 historical pairs. We evaluate six language models with Direct and ReForm prompts on all 197 inputs against final human-reviewed reference labels. GPT-6.1 Sol with Direct prompting achieves the highest reported accuracy of 0.827 and misalignment-detection F1 of 0.844; the effects of prompting vary across models. LeanReviewBench provides a testbed for reviewing semantic correspondence in existing mathematical formalization projects. LeanReviewBench is available at https://github.com/MechMath/LeanReviewBench.

PDF

item.title: When Does Reasoning Help Entity Disambiguation? Small LLMs In-Domain and Under Shift
item.description:
Authors: Samy Haffoudhi, Fabian M Suchanek, Nils Holzenberger

Subject: Computation and Language

Entity disambiguation (mapping ambiguous mentions in text to entities in a knowledge base) is a foundational step in tasks such as knowledge graph construction, question answering, and information extraction. Recent work has applied LLMs to this problem, achieving stateof-the-art performance. Notably, reasoning LLMs have been shown to perform entity disambiguation in a true zero-shot fashion, generalizing across knowledge bases and domains. However, it is unclear whether this capability survives, or remains competitive, with smaller LLMs, where entity disambiguation has typically relied on reranking rather than reasoning. We ask when reasoning is worth its cost at small scale. We compare pointwise, listwise, and reasoning-based candidate-selection components within a classical coarse-to-fine entity disambiguation pipeline, across the classical, few-shot and true zero-shot settings. The reasoning paradigm is trained with distillation and reinforcement learning recipes. The benefit of reasoning grows with domain shift: negligible in-domain, decisive in the true zero-shot setting. We show that two distinct factors are at work: the reranker's uncertainty over the candidates locates where the paradigms disagree, while shift governs which is right when they do.

PDF

item.title: Evaluating Persona Consistency in LLM User Simulators Without External Reference Annotations
item.description:
Authors: Anping Zhang, Yang Tan, Yipeng Liu, Clive Bai, Blaze Chen, Yang Li

Subject: Computation and Language

Standard evaluations assess LLM-simulated personas against an external ground truth, such as community trait annotations, but that reference is unavailable when the persona is inferred only from a short, task-oriented chat. We ask how persona consistency can be evaluated without such a reference, and propose a self-anchored internal-consistency diagnostic: the persona describes itself once and acts twice. A Likert self-report supplies a soft internal anchor; two behavioral profiles come from constrained scenario choices scored without a judge and from open-ended responses judged by an LLM. Consistency is the correlation between the self-report and each behavioral profile, in a shared six-facet BFI-2 space. The framework compares persona-construction strategies by assessing how consistently their elicited responses reflect their self-reported traits. Across ordinary-user chats (WildChat and LMSYS) and well-documented personas with community annotations (the Personality Database, PDB), profile-enriched representations agree with the anchor more closely than a raw-dialogue baseline. On PDB, this self-anchored ordering reproduces the community-annotation ordering. The pattern is stable across answering and judge models.

PDF

Comment: 21 pages

item.title: DUET: Dual-MDL Unsupervised Entropy-Trie Segmentation for Low-Resource Languages
item.description:
Authors: Xiaotian Wang, Youyuan Lin, Zhan Shen, Hitomi Yanaka

Subject: Computation and Language

Morphological segmentation, the task of decomposing words into constituent morphemes, becomes particularly challenging under extreme data scarcity, a regime that can arise in language documentation and linguistic reasoning. This difficulty stems from existing approaches' reliance on annotated data, external resources, or recurring patterns that emerge only in larger corpora. To address this limitation, we propose Dual-MDL Unsupervised Entropy-Trie Segmentation (DUET), a deterministic unsupervised algorithm that decouples structural candidate generation from statistical candidate ranking. DUET combines branching entropy with recursive paradigm discovery to generate linguistically plausible candidate segmentations, then ranks them using a dual minimum description length (MDL) criterion: a corpus-level objective rewards morpheme reuse, while a construction-tree objective guards against over-segmentation. On the SIGMORPHON 2023 interlinear glossing shared task, DUET outperforms unsupervised baselines in Morpheme F1 under both the standard and simulated extremely low-resource settings, while providing broader candidate coverage. Augmenting prompts with DUET segmentations improves performance on a linguistic reasoning benchmark, yielding the best overall results among the evaluated segmentation methods.

PDF

Comment: To appear in the Proceedings of the 20th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (EACL2027 main)

item.title: Voyag: Joint Multi-Intent Detection and Execution-Relation Classification for In-Vehicle Voice Assistants
item.description:
Authors: Sen Luo

Subject: Computation and Language

An in-vehicle voice assistant must decide not only which intents an utterance contains but also how co-active intents may be executed: concurrently, in a fixed order, or not at all without arbitration. We present Voyag, a single-forward decision model that jointly predicts ten controlled vehicle-intent slots and a three-way execution relation (parallel, sequential, mutually exclusive) over each co-active intent pair. Voyag combines a multilingual ModernBERT-style encoder (mmBERT-base, 306.9M parameters), a typed per-slot choice head, and a lightweight GroupCalibration relation head (1.61M parameters) that consumes marker hidden states, pooled context, explicit resource-requirement profiles, and symmetrized outer-product conflict features. All objectives are optimized in one joint loss: soft cross-entropy over slot choices, focal cross-entropy over relations, and a mutex-consistency penalty. On a synthetic Chinese vehicle-life benchmark with semantic scene-level splits and a leakage audit (30,017 / 3,473 / 5,000 groups), validation-only selection yields 0.9893 slot accuracy and 0.0526 expected calibration error over 50,000 slot decisions. Conditioned on gold intents, the relation head reaches 0.8548 accuracy, 0.8473 macro-F1, and 0.6062 mutually-exclusive recall over 4,000 pairs; end to end with one encoder forward it reaches 0.8530 accuracy and 0.8464 macro-F1. Against a two-stage rule pipeline, the aggregate end-to-end gain is small and borderline, so we claim no aggregate advantage; the learned head's advantage lies in sequential and parallel recall where surface rules are blind. We report rule baselines with a tautology disclosure and a held-out thermal conflict failure.

PDF

Comment: 14 pages, 1 figure, 8 tables

item.title: StutterStigma-TR: A Novel Turkish Dataset and Target-Aware BERT Framework for Stuttering-Related Stigma Detection
item.description:
Authors: Muhsin Dölek, Arezoo Sadeghzadeh

Subject: Computation and Language

Computational research on disability-related ableist harm remains limited, and condition specific resources for stuttering-related stigma are particularly scarce. This study introduces StutterStigma-TR, a Turkish dataset of 6,019 public X/Twitter posts annotated as Stigmatizing, Non-stigmatizing/contextual, or Supportive using a speech and language therapy-informed protocol with independent lived-experience evaluation. We also propose StutterStigma-BERT, a BERTurk-based target-aware framework that combines explicit target marking, target-span representation, target-conditioned context, character-level and handcrafted orthographic information, and gated discourse cues. The framework is evaluated in complementary three-class and binary settings using controlled three-seed ablation analyses and final 20-seed robustness evaluations. Under the common training protocol, Gated Discourse-OrthoTarget trained with cross-entropy is selected as the final configuration for both tasks based on internal-validation Macro-F1. Across 20 random seeds, the final three-class model achieves a mean Macro-F1 of 73.54%, while the final binary model achieves 85.17% using validation-selected decision thresholds. Task adapted harmful-language comparators are additionally evaluated under the common training protocol, and the proposed model obtains the highest mean Macro-F1 among them. For the primary three-class task, matched backbone analyses show higher internal validation Macro-F1 with BERTurk than with TurkishBERTweet or Turkish Mamba, while substantial train-validation separation persists across all three backbones. Separate direct-transfer and zero-shot experiments examine performance without StutterStigma-TR supervision. Across the task-adapted, direct-transfer, and zero-shot comparisons, the condition-specific supervised systems retain the strongest aggregate performance.

PDF

item.title: Ontology-Compiled 2D Clinical State Fields with Bidirectional Diffusion Encoders for Zero-Training Cross-Ontology Medical Coding
item.description:
Authors: Zeqiang Wang

Subject: Computation and Language

Healthcare systems continually revise clinical taxonomies, update reimbursement schedules, and harmonize cross-border registries. Existing automated coding models bind clinical text understanding to fixed vocabulary-specific heads, requiring manual relabeling and retraining whenever code sets change. We introduce Ontology-Compiled 2D Clinical State Fields (OCSF), a vocabulary-free framework that decouples clinical document reading from target ontology indexing so one trained encoder can switch across arbitrary medical vocabularies in seconds without target training. A single-pass bidirectional diffusion-pretrained encoder and vocabulary-free decoder map each clinical note into a fixed-dimension two-dimensional state matrix with zero code-specific parameters. Any target ontology is compiled offline on CPU from public text descriptions into a scale-invariant Tikhonov deconvolution operator that suppresses sibling-code interference while preserving source decision thresholds. Trained solely on English MIMIC-IV ICD-9 discharge summaries and evaluated without target tuning across 58,706 held-out test notes and five unseen ontologies spanning English ICD-10, MS-DRG, Spanish, Greek, and Chinese (115-185,458 codes), OCSF reaches 63.15% Micro-F1 on in-domain ICD-9 (outperforming a matched closed-vocabulary classifier and eliminating late-epoch tail overfitting) and transfers directly to 26,085 English ICD-10 codes (29.23% recall at gold cardinality), MS-DRG groups, and multilingual terminologies, compiling up to 185,458 codes in under 10 seconds on CPU with sub-millisecond GPU readout.

PDF

Comment: 21 pages, 4 figures, 4 main tables, 5 supplementary tables. Code available at this https URL

item.title: What Makes Good Data for Training Coding Agents? A Systematic Study on SWE-Gym
item.description:
Authors: Yikai Zhang, Mai Xu, Yunbei Zhang, Qirui Jin, Kenan Li, Yuwen Jia, Jinwei Yao, Xiangyu Zhang, Jielun Tan, Jin Pan, Zijian Jin, Xiao Sun

Subject: Computation and Language

Reinforcement learning (RL) trains coding agents on software tasks whose hidden tests decide the reward, yet task collections check these tests only against the reference fix. We ask what makes a task good training data, focusing on the correctness of its reward labels. We audit SWE-Gym with two LLM families, and a suspected error counts only if execution reproduces it. We find that unsolved often means mislabelled: 74% of the tasks that a 9B base model never solves have a test that rejects correct fixes (a false negative), versus 20% of those it sometimes solves. We repair or remove such tasks, and the audited tasks that remain train better policies.
